fields.foundation: The Seljuk Empire came out of the steppes of Central Asia in the early eleventh century. Its origins lay in the Oghuz Turkic tribal confederation that had long occupied the lands north of the Caspian and Aral Seas. The dynasty took its name from Seljuk Beg, a chieftain of the Qiniq clan of the Oghuz who, traditionally around 985 CE, converted to Sunni Islam and led his followers to the lower Syr Darya near Jand, on the frontiers of the Samanid and later Ghaznavid spheres. The conversion gave the young dynasty religious legitimacy within the Islamic world and set it apart from pagan steppe rivals. Seljuk's grandsons Tughril and Chaghri led their tribesmen into Khorasan in the 1030s, taking Merv and Nishapur in 1037–1038 and throwing off Ghaznavid authority. At the Battle of Dandanaqan in 1040 Tughril and Chaghri routed the army of the Ghaznavid sultan Masud I. The victory secured Khorasan and opened the Iranian plateau to Seljuk expansion. Tughril entered Baghdad in 1055 and freed the Abbasid caliph Al-Qa'im from the tutelage of the Shia Buyids. The caliph himself formally recognised him as sultan, a title meaning power or authority, and the steppe warlord became the temporal protector of Sunni Islam.
fields.socioeconomy: The Seljuk economy combined nomadic pastoralism, sedentary Persian agrarian traditions and the long-distance trade networks of the Islamic world. The empire lay across the principal Silk Road arteries linking China and Central Asia to the Mediterranean and the Levant, and the sultans drew substantial revenue from caravan traffic through cities such as Nishapur, Rayy, Isfahan and later, in Anatolia, Konya. Agriculture in the Iranian heartland and Mesopotamia was administered through the iqta system, a form of conditional assignment in which military commanders and officials received the revenues of specific territories in lieu of salary. The system decentralised fiscal administration while keeping up the military strength of the centre. The urban population of Iran was predominantly Persian-speaking, and the Seljuks adopted Persian as the language of administration and high culture and sponsored a revival of literature and learning. The Turkic military elite stood at the top of the social hierarchy, with Persian bureaucrats, ulama (religious scholars) and merchants forming an educated middle stratum. The madrasas endowed by the vizier Nizam al-Mulk, the Nizamiyya network, were among the most systematic educational foundations of the medieval Islamic world. They also served economic ends, since they trained the administrative and juridical class that kept the empire's institutions working across its territories.
fields.military: The Seljuk army was built around ghulams, professional slave soldiers, predominantly of Turkic origin, trained from youth in cavalry warfare and personally loyal to the sultan or senior commanders. They were supplemented by Turkmen tribal cavalry and, increasingly, by infantry levied from conquered sedentary populations. The mounted archer remained the basic tactical unit, combining the mobility of steppe warfare with the discipline of organised service. The empire's most consequential engagement was the Battle of Manzikert in August 1071, where Sultan Alp Arslan defeated the Byzantine emperor Romanos IV Diogenes and captured him alive, the first time a Byzantine emperor had been taken prisoner by a Muslim ruler. The defeat and the Byzantine civil wars that followed shattered imperial defences in Anatolia. Manzikert opened Asia Minor to Turkmen settlement and in time helped precipitate the Crusades, as Emperor Alexios I's appeal to Pope Urban II in 1095 was framed around the Turkish threat. Under Malik Shah I (r. 1072–1092) the empire campaigned across Syria, Anatolia, the Caucasus and Central Asia and received the submission of the Karakhanids of Samarkand and Kashgar. It reached an estimated maximum extent of some 3.9 million square kilometres, from the Mediterranean coast to the borders of the Chinese world. Nizam al-Mulk's Siyasat-nama set out the principles of military governance, stressing the value of a multi-ethnic professional standing army over reliance on unreliable tribal contingents.
fields.governance: The Seljuk administrative system deliberately joined Turkic military authority to Persian bureaucratic practice. It took its fullest form during the nearly thirty-year vizierate of Nizam al-Mulk (1064–1092), whose Siyasat-nama is one of the founding texts of Islamic political thought. Authority was formally divided between the sultan, who held military and temporal power, and the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad, who provided religious legitimation. This dual arrangement gave Seljuk rule ideological coherence within the Sunni world. The iqta system governed provincial administration: territory was parcelled into revenue-yielding assignments held by military governors (muqtas or muqtis), in theory non-hereditary appointees who in practice often became entrenched local powers. The Nizamiyya madrasas in Baghdad, Nishapur, Isfahan and elsewhere promoted Shafi'i jurisprudence and Ash'ari theology, and helped to standardise Sunni learning and legal practice across the empire's diverse territories. Succession, however, was never systematically regulated. By Turkic tradition sovereignty belonged to the ruling family as a whole, so that every adult male member had a legitimate claim, and the empire split after every major sultan's death. The assassination of Nizam al-Mulk in October 1092, attributed to an Ismaili Nizari agent, was followed within weeks by the death of Malik Shah. The succession warfare that resulted did damage to the empire's structure from which it never recovered.
fields.impact: The Seljuk Empire's most lasting geopolitical consequence was the Turkification and Islamisation of Anatolia. This change led in the end to the Ottoman Empire and altered the demographic character of the Middle East for a millennium. Manzikert's destruction of Byzantine power in Anatolia helped prompt the Crusades, so that the Seljuks were indirect authors of two centuries of Latin-Islamic conflict. Seljuk patronage of Persian literature, architecture and philosophy supported much intellectual work. The poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam worked under Malik Shah's patronage on the reform of the solar calendar, producing the Jalali calendar of 1079, more accurate than the contemporary Julian calendar, while the theologian al-Ghazali taught at the Baghdad Nizamiyya. The Nizamiyya network became a widely imitated model for Islamic higher education and influenced institutions from the Maghreb to Central Asia. Seljuk architectural innovations included the four-iwan mosque plan seen at the Great Mosque of Isfahan, elaborate muqarnas vaulting and monumental decorated portals, and these became the common forms of Islamic architecture from Iran to Anatolia. Trade along the Silk Road routes flourished under Seljuk protection, and the empire's commercial connections extended to Fatimid Egypt, Byzantine Constantinople, the Crusader states and the trading cities of the Indian Ocean rim.
fields.decline: The Seljuk Empire dissolved chiefly because of the way its own politics were arranged. Under the Turkic principle of dynastic patrimony, sovereignty belonged collectively to the ruling family and not to a single designated heir, so every succession could become a civil war. After Malik Shah's death in 1092 the empire broke into competing branches: the Sultanate of Rum in Anatolia, the Syrian Seljuks, the line ruling Iraq and western Iran, and the Khorasan branch under Ahmad Sanjar each went its own way. The Nizari Ismailis operated from mountain fortresses such as Alamut, seized by Hasan-i Sabbah in 1090. They destabilised government through targeted political assassination, beginning with Nizam al-Mulk in 1092, and made the highest officials of the administration insecure. The Crusader presence from 1098–1099 absorbed Seljuk military attention in the Levant, while new powers pressed from the east. The fatal blow came from the Qara Khitai, a Sinicised Khitan steppe power, who defeated Sanjar at the Battle of Qatwan in 1141. The defeat destroyed Seljuk authority in Transoxiana and fatally undermined Sanjar's prestige. In 1153 he was captured by rebellious Oghuz tribesmen, and his death in 1157 ended the eastern line. The Iraqi line staggered on through a succession of weak sultans dominated by their atabegs until Toghrul III was killed in battle by the Khwarazm Shah Tekish in 1194, and with him the Great Seljuk line ended entirely.
fields.summary: The Seljuk Empire mattered above all in two ways. It permanently changed the ethnic and religious geography of the Middle East, and as a patron it preserved, institutionalised and transmitted the intellectual and architectural traditions of classical Islamic civilisation at a moment when that civilisation faced political fragmentation.
fields.teaser: The Seljuk Turks took Baghdad in 1055 as protectors of the Abbasid caliph and crushed the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071. Their advance into Anatolia prompted the Byzantine appeal for help that launched the First Crusade.
fields.t0: Oghuz Turks from the Central Asian steppe, the Seljuks built an empire from Khorasan to the Mediterranean and became protectors of Sunni Islam.
fields.t1: Their victory at Manzikert opened Anatolia to Turkish settlement, prepared the ground for the Ottomans and helped provoke the Crusades.
fields.t2: With no fixed succession, the empire splintered after 1092; Qara Khitai and Khwarazmian blows ended the Great Seljuk line by 1194.
fields.dyk: The poet and mathematician Omar Khayyam worked under Seljuk patronage on the Jalali solar calendar of 1079, more accurate than the Julian calendar.
